title: Recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding four months after liver transplantation
purpose: Assess recurrent post-transplant bleeding and seek its source without later angiography.
decision_point: First bleeding episode four months after transplantation, after initial and repeat endoscopy but before the first angiogram or embolization. All available replies are records; the patient is not required to narrate an urgent bleeding episode.
opening: A liver-transplant recipient has recurrent vomiting of blood, dark-red rectal bleeding and right upper abdominal pain four months after transplantation. Bleeding and progressive anaemia have persisted.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Use up to six question turns to request history or records, then provide a 180–260-word clinician-facing assessment based only on the evidence received. Prioritise immediate bleeding risk, seek operative and bleeding-localisation evidence, and explain which causes require further confirmation. A specific pseudoaneurysm or fistula is not established at this decision point. facts.text: The patient is a 23-year-old man. Repeated bright-red haematemesis, about 50 mL per episode, was followed by dark-red haematochezia. Dull right upper quadrant pain, regurgitation, fatigue, dizziness, blurred vision and sweating accompanied the bleeding.

Orthotopic deceased-donor liver transplantation was performed in 2024 for end-stage alcohol-related cirrhosis. Before transplantation he had repeated decompensation and plasma exchange; oesophagogastric variceal bleeding was treated endoscopically in 2023.

The donor right hepatic artery arose from the superior mesenteric artery. Reconstruction joined donor common hepatic artery to recipient right hepatic artery and donor right hepatic artery to recipient gastroduodenal artery. The portal vein and common bile duct had end-to-end reconstruction.

Initial post-transplant immunosuppression comprised tacrolimus, enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium and corticosteroids, later adjusted. No antiplatelet or systemic anticoagulant treatment was documented in the immediate postoperative period; this does not establish the current medication list.

On postoperative days 6–8 he had fever and Enterococcus faecium bacteraemia, with positive SARS-CoV-2 testing. Fever resolved by day 9 after treatment. Imaging showed fluid collections without definite bile leakage or a localised infectious focus; bile culture was negative.

Earlier surveillance Doppler examinations showed patent hepatic arterial flow, with transient resistance or flow abnormalities that improved. No focal arterial lesion or pseudoaneurysm had been identified during that earlier surveillance.

Initial upper endoscopy found a duodenal bulb ulcer without observed active bleeding; no endoscopic haemostasis was performed. Continued bleeding prompted repeat endoscopy: removing a clot at the major duodenal papilla revealed fresh blood oozing from the papillary orifice.

Progressive anaemia during persistent bleeding is documented. A numerical blood pressure, pulse, coagulation panel and time-stamped haemoglobin specifically before the first angiogram are not supplied in this packet. Current severity measurements must be obtained rather than assumed normal.

reference:
This is recurrent overt gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive anaemia in a recent liver-transplant recipient. Dizziness, sweating and ongoing blood loss require immediate senior assessment, haemodynamic monitoring and preparation for haemorrhage management; the absence of supplied vital signs must not imply stability. Obtain current blood count, coagulation studies, crossmatch and relevant renal and graft tests while engaging gastroenterology and the transplant team.

The initial differential includes recurrent portal-hypertensive bleeding, peptic ulcer bleeding and a hepatobiliary or transplant vascular source. Prior varices create a plausible competing explanation, but neither history nor an ulcer alone localises the current bleeding. If the repeat endoscopic record is received, fresh blood from the major papilla strongly supports haemobilia and should prompt urgent vascular localisation with interventional radiology and transplant surgery. The exact lesion and arterial-biliary communication remain unconfirmed before angiography.

Review the reconstruction, immunosuppression and postoperative infectious history. Earlier patent Doppler flow does not exclude a subsequently developing vascular lesion. Past bacteraemia raises a question about infection without proving an infected pseudoaneurysm. Further diagnostic and haemostatic decisions must account for graft arterial perfusion. Do not use later embolization, surgical findings, pathology, deterioration or death to justify the initial conclusion. The later death mechanism was never definitively established; it is not a required diagnostic target.

answer:
## Assessment

This 23-year-old man presents four months after deceased-donor liver transplantation with persistent upper gastrointestinal bleeding: recurrent haematemesis (~50 mL), dark-red haematochezia, right upper quadrant pain, and progressive anaemia. Repeat endoscopy localised active bleeding to the major duodenal papilla, with fresh blood oozing from the papillary orifice after clot removal. The initial endoscopy identified a duodenal bulb ulcer without active bleeding.

**Prioritised explanations:**

1. **Hepatic artery-biliary fistula (haemobilia).** The papillary localisation combined with the reconstructed arterial anatomy (donor right hepatic artery anastomosed to the recipient gastroduodenal artery, in proximity to the end-to-end common bile duct anastomosis) makes a vascular-biliary communication the leading hypothesis. This has not been confirmed; no angiogram or cross-sectional imaging has yet been performed.

2. **Duodenal bulb ulcer.** Documented on initial endoscopy but without observed active bleeding; less likely as the primary source given the papillary localisation on repeat examination, though it may contribute.

3. **Late biliary anastomotic complication with secondary vascular erosion.** Early post-operative fluid collections and bacteraemia raise the possibility of a subclinical anastomotic problem, though no definite bile leak was identified early. This remains unconfirmed.

**Uncertainties:** Current haemoglobin, coagulation, liver function, vital signs, infection status, and anticoagulation/antiplatelet use are not documented. No biliary interventions are recorded in the interval, but absence of documentation does not exclude them.

**Proportionate next actions:** Urgent hepatic angiography to confirm or exclude a vascular source and permit embolisation; obtain current haemoglobin, coagulation profile, liver function tests, and vital signs; review current medications; assess for active infection.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: The submission is largely accurate and grounded in the supplied records: age (23-year-old man, Q4), deceased-donor transplant (Q1), duodenal bulb ulcer without active bleeding and papillary fresh blood on repeat endoscopy (Q1/Q4), arterial reconstruction details (Q2/Q5), early postoperative fluid collections and Enterococcus bacteraemia (Q3), and undocumented current labs/vitals/medications correctly flagged as unknown rather than assumed. Two weaknesses prevent a higher score: (1) it asserts the donor right hepatic artery–gastroduodenal artery anastomosis is 'in proximity to' the bile duct anastomosis, when the Q5 environment feedback explicitly states the spatial relationship is not supplied and must not be assumed; (2) it states no cross-sectional imaging 'has yet been performed', whereas the feedback says only that imaging is not supplied and this does not establish it was not performed. However, these are hedged ('has not been confirmed', 'absence of documentation does not exclude') and clinically inconsequential rather than dangerous, matching the Score 3 anchor of mostly accurate with minor inaccuracies that would not materially mislead.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The assessment at the frozen decision point accurately integrates the key available evidence: papillary bleeding localisation on repeat endoscopy, the duodenal bulb ulcer without active bleeding, the arterial reconstruction (donor right hepatic artery to recipient gastroduodenal artery), and progressive anaemia. It prioritises a hepatic artery–biliary communication as the leading hypothesis while appropriately keeping it unconfirmed, offers defensible alternatives, and clearly flags unresolved gaps (current labs, vitals, anticoagulation status, infection status). Two minor defects prevent a top score: it asserts the arterial anastomosis is 'in proximity to' the bile duct anastomosis when Q5 feedback explicitly states the spatial relationship is not supplied, and it states no cross-sectional imaging 'has yet been performed' when the packet only establishes results were not supplied. These are small unjustified closures but do not materially misframe the problem, so Score 4 applies.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the actual evidence: papillary fresh blood on repeat endoscopy (Q1/Q4 records) correctly elevates haemobilia from a transplant vascular-biliary communication to the top hypothesis, supported by the operative anatomy (Q2: donor right hepatic artery to recipient gastroduodenal artery, end-to-end common bile duct), while keeping it explicitly unconfirmed consistent with the decision point. The duodenal bulb ulcer is retained as a lower-priority alternative with correct reasoning (seen but without active bleeding), and a biliary anastomotic complication is considered using the early postoperative fluid collections and bacteraemia (Q3) without overclaiming. Dangerous mimics and immediate bleeding risk are addressed via urgent angiography and current labs/vitals. However, anchor 5 requires proportionate consideration of prior plausibility, and the submission omits recurrent portal-hypertensive/variceal bleeding despite documented 2023 variceal bleeding (Q1 record) — an important competing alternative flagged in the reference points. This omission, plus incomplete discriminating support for some alternatives, places the response at Score 4 rather than 5.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: Against the frozen candidate requirements: R2 (transplant operation, prior bleeding, postoperative/medication history) is well covered by Q1, Q2, Q5 and Q6. R3 is met: Q1 obtains the initial and repeat endoscopic findings, and Q2 requests post-bleeding imaging (ultrasound/CT) as a further localisation route, which the rubric credits even though the simulator withheld it. However, R1 is only partially fulfilled. Q3 requests current haemoglobin, coagulation and liver function tests, but no turn requests current haemodynamic observations (blood pressure, pulse) or a resuscitation/haemorrhage-team assessment, despite the presentation of persistent overt bleeding with dizziness, sweating and progressive anaemia. The acceptable alternative for R1 explicitly contemplates 'current observations plus blood count/coagulation/crossmatch, or an explicit urgent haemorrhage-team assessment'; the haemodynamic/resuscitation component is never sought within the six turns. Under the rule that an unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement caps the score at 2, and the omission does not meet the serious-failure anchor (relevant laboratory severity data were requested and some attempts were made), the appropriate score is 2.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission clearly separates established findings (papillary bleeding on repeat endoscopy, duodenal ulcer, arterial reconstruction) from unconfirmed hypotheses. It labels the hepatic artery-biliary fistula as the leading but unconfirmed hypothesis, ranks the ulcer as less likely with reasoning, and marks the biliary-complication explanation as possible but unproven. It explicitly names the sources of uncertainty (missing current haemoglobin, coagulation, vitals, infection status, anticoagulation use, absent imaging/angiography) and correctly notes that documentation gaps do not establish absence (e.g., no biliary interventions 'recorded' but not excluded). It identifies the specific next step needed to reduce the key uncertainty—urgent angiography to confirm or exclude a vascular source—plus targeted laboratory tests. This matches the Score 5 anchor: distinguishing established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions, explaining the uncertainty's source, and stating the next step to resolve it.

scores.name: Escalation/Emergency Recognition
scores.reason: The submission recognises the time-critical nature: it labels the bleeding as persistent with progressive anaemia and recommends 'urgent hepatic angiography to confirm or exclude a vascular source and permit embolisation', which is the correct escalation pathway (urgent vascular localisation via interventional radiology) for suspected haemobilia at this decision point. It also requests current haemoglobin, coagulation, liver function, vital signs, medication review and infection assessment, matching the provisional reference points. However, it stops short of a Score 5: it does not specify the care level or team pathway (e.g., immediate senior/haemorrhage-team assessment, gastroenterology and transplant surgery involvement, haemodynamic monitoring/crossmatch), and the escalation is embedded in a next-actions list rather than being prominent and unambiguous for the requested output format. Urgency is conveyed by the word 'urgent' but timing of the pathway is not otherwise elaborated. This fits Score 4: clear, timely escalation recommendation with the correct pathway specified, but without the fully specified care level and unambiguous prominence required for Score 5.

repeat_records.reason: The submission clearly recognises a serious, time-critical situation (persistent overt GI bleeding with progressive anaemia in a liver-transplant recipient) and specifies an appropriate escalation pathway: urgent hepatic angiography for localisation and embolisation, plus immediate labs and vital-sign assessment. However, it does not explicitly state senior/urgent inpatient haemorrhage-team engagement (gastroenterology, transplant surgery, interventional radiology activation), does not mention haemodynamic monitoring or resuscitation/crossmatch, and phrases urgency via 'urgent' angiography without unambiguous timing or care-level specification. This corresponds to a clear, timely escalation with a correct pathway (Score 4) but falls short of the prominent, unhedged, fully specified care level of Score 5.

The submission recognises the time-critical nature: it labels hepatic angiography as 'urgent' with a clear purpose (confirm/exclude vascular source and permit embolisation), which is the correct escalation pathway for suspected haemobilia at this decision point, and it appropriately prioritises obtaining current haemoglobin, coagulation, vital signs and infection assessment given the documented progressive anaemia (Q3/Q4 evidence). However, it falls short of a Score 5: the requested output format does not make timely escalation prominent and unambiguous, and the appropriate care level is not specified — there is no recommendation for senior/haemostasis-team review, haemodynamic monitoring, transplant-team or gastroenterology engagement, crossmatch, or an intensive/monitored care setting, despite the reference points noting dizziness, sweating and ongoing blood loss requiring immediate senior assessment. Urgency is conveyed ('urgent') and the pathway is correct, so this exceeds Score 3, but the missing care-level specification and the burial of escalation within a general action list keep it at Score 4 rather than 5.

scores.name: Chronological precision
scores.reason: The submission presents events in correct sequence with explicit temporal anchors: transplantation 'four months' prior, initial endoscopy followed by repeat endoscopy with papillary localisation, and earlier postoperative complications referenced as historical context. The order of endoscopies (initial ulcer finding, then repeat papillary bleeding) matches the Q1/Q4 records, and no events are presented out of sequence. Minor sequencing errors (score 3) are absent. This satisfies the score 5 anchor: correct chronology with explicit temporal anchors such as 'four months after transplantation'.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.

Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. evaluation_input.answer:
## Assessment

This 23-year-old man presents four months after deceased-donor liver transplantation with persistent upper gastrointestinal bleeding: recurrent haematemesis (~50 mL), dark-red haematochezia, right upper quadrant pain, and progressive anaemia. Repeat endoscopy localised active bleeding to the major duodenal papilla, with fresh blood oozing from the papillary orifice after clot removal. The initial endoscopy identified a duodenal bulb ulcer without active bleeding.

**Prioritised explanations:**

1. **Hepatic artery-biliary fistula (haemobilia).** The papillary localisation combined with the reconstructed arterial anatomy (donor right hepatic artery anastomosed to the recipient gastroduodenal artery, in proximity to the end-to-end common bile duct anastomosis) makes a vascular-biliary communication the leading hypothesis. This has not been confirmed; no angiogram or cross-sectional imaging has yet been performed.

2. **Duodenal bulb ulcer.** Documented on initial endoscopy but without observed active bleeding; less likely as the primary source given the papillary localisation on repeat examination, though it may contribute.

3. **Late biliary anastomotic complication with secondary vascular erosion.** Early post-operative fluid collections and bacteraemia raise the possibility of a subclinical anastomotic problem, though no definite bile leak was identified early. This remains unconfirmed.

**Uncertainties:** Current haemoglobin, coagulation, liver function, vital signs, infection status, and anticoagulation/antiplatelet use are not documented. No biliary interventions are recorded in the interval, but absence of documentation does not exclude them.

**Proportionate next actions:** Urgent hepatic angiography to confirm or exclude a vascular source and permit embolisation; obtain current haemoglobin, coagulation profile, liver function tests, and vital signs; review current medications; assess for active infection.

evaluation_input.reference:
This is recurrent overt gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive anaemia in a recent liver-transplant recipient. Dizziness, sweating and ongoing blood loss require immediate senior assessment, haemodynamic monitoring and preparation for haemorrhage management; the absence of supplied vital signs must not imply stability. Obtain current blood count, coagulation studies, crossmatch and relevant renal and graft tests while engaging gastroenterology and the transplant team.

The initial differential includes recurrent portal-hypertensive bleeding, peptic ulcer bleeding and a hepatobiliary or transplant vascular source. Prior varices create a plausible competing explanation, but neither history nor an ulcer alone localises the current bleeding. If the repeat endoscopic record is received, fresh blood from the major papilla strongly supports haemobilia and should prompt urgent vascular localisation with interventional radiology and transplant surgery. The exact lesion and arterial-biliary communication remain unconfirmed before angiography.

Review the reconstruction, immunosuppression and postoperative infectious history. Earlier patent Doppler flow does not exclude a subsequently developing vascular lesion. Past bacteraemia raises a question about infection without proving an infected pseudoaneurysm. Further diagnostic and haemostatic decisions must account for graft arterial perfusion. Do not use later embolization, surgical findings, pathology, deterioration or death to justify the initial conclusion. The later death mechanism was never definitively established; it is not a required diagnostic target.
